eyebrow: Travel like a Roi Et local · Updated 2026
intro: Roi Et is an Isan city with treasures scattered from the town center to the far paddies — a 101-meter observation tower shaped like a whot, a huge lake in the heart of town, a white grand chedi on a mountain, Luang Pho Yai the tallest standing Buddha in Thailand, all the way out to the Isan Sea and the legendary Thung Kula Rong Hai. Here are the 10 attractions real visitors talk about most, with entry fees, locations, and trip-planning tips. Loop the town in a single day or drive out overnight to collect the mountain temple and the rice plains — it all fits.
chips: 🌳 Bueng Phlan Chai lake park downtown
🙏 Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha

blocks.html:
Roi Et's charm is that it's "an easygoing city to explore, with standout sights scattered across the whole province." Many of the big names cluster in the town center around Bueng Phlan Chai, the island lake park that serves as the city's lungs — you could stroll, pedal a swan boat, and feed the fish there all day. On one side of the lake rises Whot 101 Tower, a sky-high observation tower shaped like the whot, the Isan panpipe, where you can take in the entire city in 360 degrees. Come evening, the town center offers Saket Nakhon Walking Street and Wat Pa Kung for eating and shopping on foot. If your tastes run to blessings and views, drive out of town to pay respects at Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon on the mountain in Nong Phok, stop by Luang Pho Yai at Wat Burapha Phiram, and go laze on the white-sand beach at Bueng Kluea — a genuine inland Isan Sea. Temple pilgrims, city wanderers, nature lovers, and history buffs can all string a trip together here.

This list includes the pins you should not miss in Roi Et: Whot 101 Tower, the 101-meter observation tower with a glass-floor skywalk on floor 34 overlooking Bueng Phlan Chai and the whole town; Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon at Wat Pha Nam Thip, the white grand chedi with gold detailing measuring 101 meters per side across 6 floors, designed by the Fine Arts Department; and Luang Pho Yai at Wat Burapha Phiram, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha in the blessing-granting posture, visible from far away. Out of town there's also Bueng Kluea, with a white-sand beach nearly a kilometer long that people call the Isan Sea; Prang Ku and Ku Ka Sing, monuments of Khmer art; and Thung Kula Rong Hai, the famed jasmine-rice country with paddy views to the horizon. Scroll on for the details, point by point, and plot your own route.

blocks.name: Whot 101 Tower (Roi Et Observation Tower)
blocks.area: Nai Mueang, Mueang Roi Et district
blocks.signature: A 101-meter observation tower shaped like a whot, the Isan panpipe — ride the lift to the 360-degree viewpoint on floor 31 and the glass-floor skywalk on floor 34, overlooking Bueng Phlan Chai and the entire city
blocks.descHtml:
If you visit Roi Et and skip Whot 101 Tower, it barely counts as having been here. This is the landmark you can spot from far away — a city observation tower shaped like a "whot", the traditional Isan panpipe, standing 101 meters tall to match the province's number. It sits in Somdet Phra Srinagarindra Park right beside Bueng Phlan Chai in the heart of town, and it's perfect for anyone who wants to see all of Roi Et from an angle you can't get anywhere else — whether you come solo, with family, or as a couple collecting beautiful views.

The can't-miss highlight is taking the lift up to the air-conditioned 360-degree viewing room on floor 31, where you can see Bueng Phlan Chai, the town, and the rice fields in every direction, then continuing to the clear glass-floor skywalk on floor 34 — plenty of visitors admit their legs went wobbly, but loved every second. That aerial view is what reviewers talk about most. If you're feeling brave, there's now a zipline and a tower jump as well, while those who prefer to take it easy can browse the city museum, cafe, and souvenir shops inside the building.

Admission is ฿50 for adults, ฿40 for students and seniors, with free entry for young children and the very elderly — a fair price for the view you get. It's open roughly 9am to 6pm every day, sits right in the city center, is easy to reach, and has plenty of parking according to many reviews. For the best light, come in the late afternoon near sunset, when the city slowly switches over to its night lights — genuinely beautiful.

A couple of things to know: on long weekends and Saturdays–Sundays it gets crowded and you may queue for the lift, and the outdoor viewing deck is quite windy — anyone scared of heights will need a moment on the glass floor. Overall, though, it's excellent value, and well worth a stop whenever you pass through Roi Et.
mustOrder: 360-degree viewpoint on floor 31
Glass-floor skywalk on floor 34
Sunset views over Bueng Phlan Chai
Zipline / tower jump for thrill-seekers
blocks.bestFor: Late afternoon–sunset views; the city's first landmark stop

blocks.name: Bueng Phlan Chai
blocks.area: Nai Mueang, Mueang Roi Et district
blocks.signature: A huge island lake park in the heart of the city — stroll, pedal swan boats, feed the fish, with the City Pillar Shrine and a fitness park; the lungs and gathering place of Roi Et
blocks.descHtml:
Ask a local where to go for a stroll in Roi Et and nearly everyone gives the same answer: "Bueng Phlan Chai" — a huge lake park in the middle of the city that serves as both the lungs and the living room of the whole province. The lake is vast, with a central island landscaped into flower gardens, shaded by big trees, and circled by a walking–running–cycling path of roughly 2 kilometers. It suits families, exercise lovers, and travelers who want to soak up the city at an easy pace.

The highlights you shouldn't miss: pedal a boat out on the lake and feed the fish (rentals are inexpensive), walk across the bridge to pay respects at the City Pillar Shrine that Roi Et people revere, and stop by the large walking Buddha statue set among the flower gardens, the flower clock, and the miniature waterfall. Kids get a playground and a fitness park to run around in, and if you want a bird's-eye view, walk a little further to the 101 observation tower, which looks down over the entire lake.

Real reviews agree that the park is clean and well kept, with plenty of parking, decent lighting, good safety, and photogenic corners everywhere. Many say the evening is when it really comes alive — people jogging, playing basketball and futsal, or just sitting by the water in the cool breeze. Some foreign reviewers even compare it to Lumphini Park in Bangkok.

As for entry, walking in is completely free and the park is open 24 hours, though early morning and evening are the popular times. It sits in Nai Mueang subdistrict, Mueang Roi Et — dead center of town, convenient for everything. Small things to know: in the rainy season the water can get a little murky, and if you want to feed the fish or pedal a boat, come between midday and evening when the rental stands are open. Bring an umbrella or hat if you visit under the midday sun.
mustOrder: Pedal a boat and feed the fish mid-lake
Pay respects at the City Pillar Shrine
Walk or jog the ~2 km loop around the lake
Photograph the flower gardens on the central island
blocks.bestFor: Morning and evening strolls or workouts — great for the whole family

blocks.name: Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon (Wat Pha Nam Thip Thep Prasit Wanaram)
blocks.area: Pha Nam Yoi, Nong Phok district, Roi Et
blocks.signature: A magnificent white grand chedi with gold detailing — 101 meters wide, long, and tall across 6 floors, set on a mountaintop and designed by the Fine Arts Department; explore every floor and take in sweeping forest views
blocks.descHtml:
Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon at Wat Pha Nam Thip Thep Prasit Wanaram is a magnificent white grand chedi with gold detailing, crowning a green mountaintop in the Phu Phan range in Nong Phok district, about 80 kilometers from Roi Et town. Designed by the Fine Arts Department, it's a contemporary work blending Phra Pathom Chedi with Phra That Phanom, measuring 101 meters in width, length, and height (around 109 meters including the golden spire), with 6 floors in total and small chedis surrounding it at all 8 compass points. It's ideal for temple-goers, people praying for good fortune, lovers of beautiful architecture, and families after wide mountain views.

The highlight most people mention is walking up through it floor by floor — each level is decorated with stucco patterns and gold so intricate it feels like standing in a celestial palace. A lift serves almost every floor except the topmost, which you climb on foot. Real reviews agree the view from the top is stunning, with green forested hills stretching as far as the eye can see, especially on a clear day. The atmosphere up there is quiet and breezy — a lovely place to sit and let your mind rest — and hardly anyone leaves without a photo of the white chedi against the sky.

Entry is free, open daily from about 06:00–18:00 (some periods list 08:00–17:00). Good to know: you park in the lot at the base and take the temple's shuttle up to the chedi itself, as the road up is quite steep mountain terrain. Allow extra travel time and pick a clear day for the most rewarding views. Dress modestly since it's a sacred site, and budget around 1–2 hours for the visit.

It's popular because it's Roi Et's signature landmark, one of the most beautiful grand chedis in all of Isan, and deeply revered by people in the area. On Google Maps it scores around 4.7 from more than a thousand reviewers, many saying it exceeded expectations and was worth the long drive. If you're passing through Roi Et, make a point of seeing it at least once.
mustOrder: Walk through all 6 floors of the white-and-gold grand chedi
Climb to the top floor for sweeping views over green hills
The ring of 8 smaller chedis around the main one
Ride the temple shuttle up the mountain
blocks.bestFor: Temple-goers praying for good fortune + mountaintop views
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Seksan Phonsuwan via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

blocks.name: Wat Burapha Phiram (Luang Pho Yai — Phra Phuttha Rattana Mongkhon Maha Muni)
blocks.area: Nai Mueang, Mueang Roi Et district
blocks.signature: A royal temple housing Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha in the blessing-granting posture — 59 meters 20 cm from head to foot, visible from afar, with a museum in the statue's base
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Burapha Phiram is a royal temple in the middle of Roi Et town that everyone ends up visiting, because it is home to "Luang Pho Yai" — Phra Phuttha Rattana Mongkhon Maha Muni, the tallest standing Buddha in the blessing-granting posture in Thailand. The statue alone measures 59 meters 20 centimeters from head to foot, or nearly 68 meters including the base — as tall as a building dozens of stories high and visible from almost every corner of the city. It's a natural stop for anyone who wants to pray for blessings, merit-makers, families bringing older relatives, and travelers ticking off the province's landmarks.

The must-do moment is walking in to stand beneath Luang Pho Yai and looking straight up. Review after review says the same thing: "up close, he's too big to fit in the frame" — you have to back way up to capture the whole statue. There's a museum in the base of the statue to explore, a chedi enshrining relics of the Buddha behind it, and a reclining Buddha resting under a large tree in a little grotto-like nook, along with Buddha images for every day of the week to pay respects to. One lap around covers both your prayers and your photos.

The temple grounds are spacious, shady, and clean; real reviews praise the convenient parking and the easy, mostly stair-free walking. Entry is free — there are just donation boxes and flower-and-incense stalls if you wish — so the actual cost is close to zero. It's open daily from around 05:00 in the early morning until about 19:00, on Phadung Phanit Road in Nai Mueang, only a few kilometers from the town center and bus terminal — easy to reach by car or songthaew.

The temple is popular because it's both the city's sacred guardian and an unmistakable photo spot, scoring around 4.4 on Google from several hundred reviews and consistently ranking near the top of Roi Et's attractions. Small tips: it's a religious site, so dress modestly, and the morning and late-afternoon light is gentler — better for photographing the statue than harsh midday. If it's your first time in Roi Et, this should be the first pin on your map.
mustOrder: Stand beneath Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha (59.20 m)
The museum at the base of the statue
Pay respects to the reclining Buddha under the big tree + birthday Buddhas
The relic chedi behind the main statue
blocks.bestFor: First stop of a Roi Et trip — merit-makers and families bringing elders to pray for blessings
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Supanut Arunoprayote / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

blocks.name: Bueng Kluea (the Isan Sea)
blocks.area: Bueng Kluea, Selaphum district, Roi Et
blocks.signature: A vast 7,500-rai freshwater lake with a white-sand beach nearly 1 km long — hence the nickname 'the Isan Sea' — plus floating Isan restaurant rafts, swimming, and water sports
blocks.priceRange: Free entry (pay for food/boat rentals as used)
blocks.descHtml:
If you think Roi Et has no seaside, come see "Bueng Kluea" — known locally as the Isan Sea — and you may change your mind. It's a very large freshwater lake of around 7,500 rai (roughly 12 sq km) that holds water all year round, and what earns it the "sea" nickname is the white sandy beach stretching nearly 1 kilometer along its western shore. Strolling the beach with the water reaching to the horizon and a cool breeze blowing genuinely feels like a trip to the coast — right in the middle of Isan. It suits families bringing kids for a swim, groups of friends looking to unwind, and anyone after a quiet corner close to nature.

The must-try highlight is the floating restaurant rafts lined up along the shore: order bold Isan food — som tam, grilled fish, koi, larb — and eat while gazing out over the water. Kids love the pedal boats and caterpillar boats out on the lake, and swimmers can wade in from the sandy beach. The vibe is easygoing and homespun rather than fancy, but you get warmth and full-on natural scenery. Late afternoon is when most people come, as the heat softens and the lakeside sunset is beautiful.

Budget-wise it's very light: entry to the area is free with no admission fee — you pay only for food on the rafts and pedal-boat or water-play rentals as you use them, and it's even better value shared among a group. It's in Bueng Kluea subdistrict, Selaphum district, a fair drive from Roi Et town, open daily roughly 09:00–18:00 (some food rafts start closing in the early evening).

A few things to know: the lake is also a wild waterfowl conservation area, with waterbirds arriving in the cool season — please help keep it clean and don't drop litter into the lake. Water levels and beach width change with the seasons; in the dry season the beach is wider and better for swimming. The midday sun is quite strong, so bringing a hat and umbrella makes things much more comfortable.
mustOrder: Stroll the nearly 1-km white-sand beach
Eat Isan food on a floating raft
Pedal boats / caterpillar boats
Watch the sunset over the lake in the evening
blocks.bestFor: Families and groups — Isan food on a floating raft with evening views

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Roi Et — Downtown by the Lake or Near the Whot Tower
blocks.text: To get the most out of Roi Et, stay a night: stroll along Bueng Phlan Chai in the evening, ride up Whot 101 Tower to watch the city at sunset, and visit Luang Pho Yai in the quiet early morning before the crowds. The most popular places to stay cluster in central Roi Et around Bueng Phlan Chai, within easy walking distance of the Whot tower, Saket Nakhon Walking Street, and Wat Pa Kung. There are both downtown hotels and boutique-style stays — pick a location close to your first morning's sights and you'll get the most out of it. Compare prices and reviews before you book.

blocks.name: Saket Nakhon Walking Street
blocks.area: Ratchupakan Road, Nai Mueang, Mueang Roi Et district, Roi Et
blocks.cuisine: Isan local food / Street food / Handmade goods
blocks.signature: A cultural walking street in the city center with a laid-back vibe — handmade stalls, Isan local food, snacks, and live music; graze and shop on foot in the evening
blocks.descHtml:
If your Roi Et visit happens to land on a Friday or Saturday evening, locals will point you to "Saket Nakhon Walking Street" first — the province's biggest cultural walking street, right in the city center. The name "Saket Nakhon" comes from Roi Et's old name in the Urangkhathat legend, meaning the city of one hundred and one gates, and it has become a market name locals wear with pride. The atmosphere is relaxed and easy to wander — good for foodies, handmade-goods shoppers, and families bringing the kids out for an evening stroll.

The don't-miss draw is the spread of Isan local food and snacks on offer everywhere — savory dishes, sweets, fresh fruit juices, and herbal drinks. Plenty of real reviews praise how clearly the market is zoned into food and clothing sections, making it easy to navigate. Another corner many people love is the handmade stalls and youth fashion at friendly prices, and on some nights there's live music to enjoy as you browse. This is a market Roi Et people actually come to themselves — not just a tourist bazaar.

Budget-wise it's very easy: entry is free, and a hundred baht or so of grazing and shopping fills you up. It's centrally located on Ratchupakan Road in Nai Mueang, Mueang Roi Et district, near Robinson mall and Bueng Phlan Chai, with parking not hard to find nearby. It runs in the evening through early night, roughly 16:00–21:00, mainly on Fridays and Saturdays — come around dusk when all the stalls are out and the air has cooled down.

One small caveat: opening days and hours can shift with the seasons and the organizers' announcements, and the market occasionally gets a facelift or moves location — check its Facebook page before you go so you don't miss out. Friday and Saturday evenings are when it's liveliest and fullest.
mustOrder: Isan local dishes and snacks
Fresh fruit juices and herbal drinks
Handmade stalls and fashion clothing
Stroll to live music in the evening
blocks.bestFor: Friday–Saturday evenings; easygoing foodies and families grazing and shopping
blocks.zone: City center (near Bueng Phlan Chai & Robinson)
blocks.hours: ~16:00–21:00, mainly Fri–Sat (check the page before going)

blocks.name: Wat Prachakhom Wanaram (Wat Pa Kung)
blocks.signature: A grand sandstone stupa modeled after Borobudur, built by Luang Pu Si Mahaviro
blocks.descHtml:
If you thought you had to fly to Indonesia to see a Borobudur-style stupa, stop by Wat Pa Kung in Si Somdet district first. It's home to a massive sandstone stupa directly inspired by the great Borobudur. The story goes that Luang Pu Si Mahaviro, a revered meditation monk of Roi Et, traveled to Borobudur on a religious mission in 1988 and was so struck by its grandeur that he began building this chedi in 1992.

What people talk about most is that the stupa is built from natural sandstone — said to be the first large sandstone chedi in Thailand. The walls around the chedi are carved with scenes from the Buddha's life and the Vessantara Jataka, and it's a pleasure to work through them panel by panel. Enshrined inside are relics of the Buddha brought from India, and the spiritually inclined often come to pay respects to Luang Pu Si here too, as he has long been venerated across Isan.

The overall setting is a forest temple — shady, quiet, and calm — better suited to those seeking a peaceful corner than a bustling temple crowd. It's especially beautiful in the early morning and late afternoon when the sun is soft and the color of the sandstone stands out against the sky — a treat for anyone who loves photographing architecture. Dress modestly as it's temple grounds, and allow a little time to study the carvings around the chedi so you don't rush past the good parts.

Getting here from Roi Et town toward Si Somdet district isn't far — driving yourself is easiest, there's a large parking lot, and entry is free with no admission fee. If your Roi Et itinerary leans temples and blessings, this is a pin you shouldn't skip.
blocks.bestFor: Spiritual visitors, temple fans, and photographers of sandstone-chedi architecture
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Charin ninsu / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)
mustOrder: The Borobudur-style sandstone grand stupa
Carvings of the Buddha's life and the Vessantara Jataka around the chedi
Pay respects to the Buddha relics enshrined inside
Ask blessings from Luang Pu Si Mahaviro

blocks.name: Prang Ku (Prasat Nong Ku)
blocks.area: Ma-ue, Thawat Buri district, Roi Et
blocks.signature: A laterite Khmer monument in the arokayasala (hospital chapel) style, registered as a national historic site — a history-lover's photo stop close to town
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to collect a Khmer-era monument without driving far from Roi Et town, "Prang Ku" — known locally as "Prasat Nong Ku" — is the perfect pin. It sits within Wat Si Rattanaram in Ban Yang Ku, Ma-ue subdistrict, Thawat Buri district, only 10-odd kilometers from town: a short drive out toward Roi Et airport, then a quick turn down a lane. It suits history lovers, people who enjoy photographing old ruins, and families wanting a quiet stop along the way. The prang is built of laterite from the era of King Jayavarman VII, roughly a thousand years old, part of a group of buildings believed to be an "arokayasala" — a hospital chapel of the ancient Khmer empire. The Fine Arts Department registered it as a national historic monument back in 1935.

The highlight is the main laterite prang standing prominently in the temple courtyard, ringed by a boundary wall with a gopura gateway at the front. Nearby are a square library building and a laterite pond (baray) by the entrance, where many visitors hunt for shots of the prasat reflected in the water. Most traveler reviews agree it's a small Khmer sanctuary in fairly complete condition; inside the prang is a Buddha image you can pay respects to, and a full walk around takes less than an hour.

The overall mood is quiet, calm, and shaded, since it sits within temple grounds. Entry is free with no charge, parking is convenient, and it's open daily roughly 08:00–18:00. The liveliest time is the annual "Bun Song Ku" festival that villagers hold around the fifth lunar month (full moon), with a ritual bathing ceremony and local activities to watch — come then if you want to see it at its busiest.

Small things to know: it's a historic site within temple grounds, so dress modestly and help keep it clean. The prasat isn't large — if you make it your only destination it may feel small, but woven into a Roi Et trip alongside the province's other Khmer monuments it's well worth it, delivering the full history-trail mood. Morning or late afternoon, when the sun is soft, is the best time for photos and comfortable walking.
mustOrder: The main Khmer-style laterite prang in the temple courtyard
The library, boundary wall, and gopura gateway
The laterite pond (baray) out front
The 1935 national historic monument plaque
blocks.bestFor: History fans photographing ancient ruins — a short stop near town
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Adriaan Castermans (via Panoramio) / Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.name: Ku Ka Sing
blocks.area: Ku Ka Sing, Kaset Wisai district, Roi Et
blocks.signature: A fairly large, well-preserved laterite Khmer temple complex with a main prang and boundary wall — Roi Et's open-air classroom of Khmer history
blocks.descHtml:
If you drive down to the south of Roi Et around Thung Kula Rong Hai, "Ku Ka Sing" is a pin no history lover should miss — a fairly large Khmer temple complex still in good condition, set inside Wat Burapha Ku Ka Sing in Ban Ku Ka Sing, Kaset Wisai district. It suits anyone who enjoys ancient monuments, poring over old craftsmanship, or learning Isan's Khmer history without jostling crowds; families and casual visitors can wander comfortably too, thanks to the wide, shaded grounds within the temple.

The unmissable highlight is the three prangs set in a row on a single laterite base along a north–south line, facing east, with the largest central prang — which once housed a shiva linga — flanked by two library buildings (viharas), all enclosed by a boundary wall with gateways at the four cardinal points and a horseshoe-shaped moat. The structures are built of laterite and brick, decorated with sandstone carvings of lotus petals, apsara dancers, rishi hermits, and miniature prangs on the corners of the tiered roofs — Khmer art in the Baphuon–Bayon style, dating to the 16th Buddhist century (around the 11th century CE). It was originally built as a Hindu sanctuary dedicated to Shiva, and the 1990 excavation even turned up a Ganesha figure, a sandstone shiva linga, and gold ornaments.

The atmosphere is the quiet calm of a provincial historic site — never crowded. Most reviews praise its step-back-in-time mood; you can still read the original beauty and grandeur, and while some prang tops have crumbled with time, the main structures remain complete and well restored by the Fine Arts Department. There's no entry fee, it's open daily during daylight hours, and there's parking inside the temple.

Good to know: it's a fair distance from Roi Et town — take Highway 214 toward Kaset Wisai, then another 10 kilometers or so into the village. Come in the morning or late afternoon for softer light, better photos, and cooler walking, and dress modestly since it's on temple grounds. This area is also part of the Thung Kula Rong Hai community, famous for jasmine rice and silk, so after the prasat you can wander into local village life too.
mustOrder: Three prangs on a single laterite base, facing east
The boundary wall + gopura gateways at all four cardinal points
The horseshoe-shaped moat around the sanctuary
Sandstone carvings — lotus petals, apsaras, and miniature prangs on the roof corners
blocks.bestFor: Khmer-history buffs + a Thung Kula Rong Hai trip; come morning or late afternoon
blocks.zone: Kaset Wisai (Thung Kula Rong Hai, southern Roi Et)
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Dominique Dalbiez (Ddalbiez) / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 3.0

blocks.name: Thung Kula Rong Hai
blocks.signature: The legendary great plain of Isan, home of premium jasmine rice — rice-field views to the horizon, wide-open photo spots, and authentic hom mali rice to buy
blocks.descHtml:
Thung Kula Rong Hai is the legendary great plain of Isan, spanning more than 2 million rai (around 3,200 sq km) across 5 provinces; on the Roi Et side, the most visited stretches are around Kaset Wisai and Suwannaphum districts in the province's south. The name sounds sorrowful — "the plain where the Kula wept" — because it was once said to be so parched and barren that even the wandering Kula traders couldn't make it across. Today it has transformed into the most celebrated jasmine-rice country in Thailand: the salty, sandy soil and the local climate make the rice exceptionally fragrant, earning it GI registration. It's made for road-trippers who want rice-field views stretching to the horizon, and anyone keen to bring authentic hom mali rice home.

The highlight is the sheer sweep of paddies running to where sky meets earth. The most beautiful window is the late rainy season into early winter, around November–December, when the rice ripens golden across the whole plain. Reviewers on Pantip describe driving the Kaset Wisai roads and pulling over again and again for photos along the paddy bunds; at dawn a thin mist floats over the fields, and in the evening golden light falls on the rice ears — stunning. Don't miss the wide-field photos, a stop at Kuchinarai / community rice shops to buy genuine Thung Kula jasmine rice, and if you come at harvest time you'll see real farming life in motion.

It's open country — no entry fee, no gates, accessible all day — though morning and late afternoon are best since the midday sun is fierce and hot. It lies well outside Roi Et town, so drive yourself or rent a car: the photo spots are scattered along paddy bunds and country roads rather than gathered at one central point. The "Thung Kula Rong Hai at Kaset Wisai" Facebook page posts regular updates on the fields and local activities — worth checking before you go.

It's popular because it's the true image of Isan — wide fields, clear skies, fragrant rice, and a legend that makes people want to see it with their own eyes. Know that this is a views-and-atmosphere destination, not a place with full facilities: bring water, a hat, and sunscreen, and keep the fuel tank topped up, since gas stations and shops are spread thin. Come in the green-rice or golden-rice season for the most rewarding views.
mustOrder: Photograph rice fields stretching to the horizon
See the paddies turn golden (Nov–Dec)
Buy authentic Thung Kula jasmine rice to take home
Catch the morning mist / evening light along the paddy bunds
blocks.bestFor: Road-trippers who love wide rice-field views + buying real jasmine rice; best morning–evening

blocks.title: Know Before You Go — Roi Et

items.title: Driving yourself or renting a car works best
items.text: The sights in central Roi Et are within walking distance of each other, but Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon, Bueng Kluea, and Thung Kula Rong Hai lie outside town in different directions, and public transport is limited. The easiest option is renting a car or motorbike — Grab is very scarce in Roi Et, so sort out your wheels before heading out of town.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Temples, the food stalls at Saket Nakhon Walking Street and Wat Pa Kung, and the pedal-boat rentals at Bueng Phlan Chai mostly take cash. Keep small notes handy for the Whot 101 Tower entry fee, parking, roadside snacks, and temple donation boxes. ATMs are easy to find in town but sparse at the attractions outside it.

items.title: Go up the Whot tower in the late afternoon for the best views
items.text: The midday sun in Roi Et is strong. Ride up Whot 101 Tower in the late afternoon and you'll see the town and Bueng Phlan Chai at sunset, which is far prettier. Saket Nakhon Walking Street runs evenings only and Wat Pa Kung opens Friday–Sunday, so plan your days accordingly if you're set on going.

items.title: Dress modestly when visiting temples
items.text: Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon and Wat Burapha Phiram (Luang Pho Yai) are sacred places where people genuinely come to worship. Cover shoulders and knees, remove your shoes where signs indicate, and keep your voice down inside the vihara and chedi areas.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Outside the main tourist spots, English signs and menus are scarce. Keep a translation app handy, or simply point at pictures in the markets and Isan eateries — it works. Most Roi Et people are kind and patient with travelers.

items.title: Pick up authentic jasmine rice at Thung Kula
items.text: Thung Kula Rong Hai is a famed source of premium jasmine rice. If you drive south to Kaset Wisai–Suwannaphum, stop and buy Thung Kula hom mali rice as a gift to take home — a signature local product unlike anywhere else.

blocks.title: Planning the Most Rewarding Roi Et Trip
blocks.html:
Roi Et is easy to explore because the town's headline sights cluster around Bueng Phlan Chai: stroll the lakeside, pedal a boat, then cross over to ride up Whot 101 Tower for 360-degree city views and the glass-floor skywalk — all in one neighborhood. That leaves Luang Pho Yai at Wat Burapha Phiram, also in town, so half a day covers the lot. Come evening, continue to Saket Nakhon Walking Street (evenings only) or Wat Pa Kung, open Friday–Sunday, and graze your way through Isan food at an easy pace.

With more than a day, head out of town. Temple-goers and view-chasers should aim for Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon at Wat Pha Nam Thip in Nong Phok district, on a mountain to the northeast — a 6-floor white grand chedi you can climb for forest views. Swimmers and loungers should make for Bueng Kluea, the Isan Sea, in Selaphum district, with its white-sand beach and floating restaurant rafts. And history and rice-field fans can drive south to Kaset Wisai to collect Ku Ka Sing, Prang Ku, and Thung Kula Rong Hai with its horizon-wide views in one run. Group your out-of-town stops by direction and you'll save the most time.

blocks.text: Roi Et is fun even as a day trip, but stay a night in the city center and you can stroll Bueng Phlan Chai in the evening, watch the sunset over town from the Whot tower, then drive out the next morning to pay respects at the grand chedi or laze on the beach at Bueng Kluea. faq.q: Which Roi Et attractions should I not miss?
faq.a: The pins visitors rarely skip are Whot 101 Tower, the 101-meter whot-shaped observation tower in the city center with its glass-floor skywalk; Bueng Phlan Chai, the island lake park in the heart of town; Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon at Wat Pha Nam Thip in Nong Phok district, a white grand chedi on a mountain; Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha, at Wat Burapha Phiram; and Bueng Kluea, the Isan Sea, in Selaphum district.

faq.q: What are the highlights of Roi Et?
faq.a: Roi Et's signature is the number 101, woven into several of its sights: Whot 101 Tower, a 101-meter observation tower with 360-degree city views and a skywalk on floor 34, and Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon, measuring 101 meters in width, length, and height across 6 floors on a mountaintop, designed by the Fine Arts Department. Add Luang Pho Yai, Thailand's tallest standing Buddha in the blessing-granting posture at over 59 meters from head to foot, and Bueng Kluea with its nearly kilometer-long white-sand beach that people call the Isan Sea.

faq.q: Are Roi Et attractions expensive to enter?
faq.a: Most are free or cost very little. Bueng Phlan Chai is free (pedal boats around ฿50), Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon and Wat Burapha Phiram (Luang Pho Yai) are free to visit, Prang Ku, Ku Ka Sing, and Thung Kula Rong Hai charge no entry, Bueng Kluea is free with you paying only for food or boat rentals, and Saket Nakhon Walking Street and Wat Pa Kung are free — while Whot 101 Tower charges about ฿50 for adults.

faq.q: How do I get to and around Roi Et, and is parking easy?
faq.a: Roi Et has coaches from Bangkok and an airport with domestic flights, but once you arrive, driving yourself or renting a car is easiest since public transport within the province is limited. The in-town sights — Whot 101 Tower, Bueng Phlan Chai, and Wat Burapha Phiram — sit close together and have parking lots, while Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon in Nong Phok, Bueng Kluea in Selaphum, and Thung Kula Rong Hai–Ku Ka Sing in Kaset Wisai lie outside town in different directions, so arrange your transport before heading out.

faq.q: What are the opening hours of Roi Et's attractions?
faq.a: Temples like Phra Maha Chedi Chai Mongkhon and Wat Burapha Phiram open from daytime until evening — mornings are quieter with gentler sun. Whot 101 Tower keeps set hours from daytime into the evening; come late in the day to see the town at sunset. Bueng Phlan Chai can be strolled all day, Saket Nakhon Walking Street runs evenings only, and Wat Pa Kung opens Friday–Sunday until around 10:30pm. Double-check each place's hours before setting out, as they can shift on holidays.
